title: Great Rift Valley
description: Continuous geographic trench from Asia to Southeast Africa
wiki_lead:
The Great Rift Valley (GRV) is a series of contiguous geographic depressions, approximately 6,500 kilometres (4,000 mi) in total length, which, in its original definition, runs from "the plains of northern Syria" in the north, through the Red Sea, to Mozambique in the south. The term remains in use in the fields of geography, zoology, ecology, paleontology and other disciplines, but it is now rarely used in geology where the term "Afro-Arabian Rift System" is preferred, which describes the series of geological structures that have given rise to the geographical feature. Great Rift Valley is also often used to refer to valleys, such as the Kenyan Rift Valley, within the East African Rift system.
The term was introduced by British geologist John Walter Gregory in 1896, following on from the work of Austrian geologist Eduard Suess, who first proposed the existence of a linked set of features extending from Syria to Mozambique.

The Great Rift Valley (GRV) is a series of contiguous geographic depressions, approximately 6,500 kilometres (4,000 mi) in total length, which, in its original definition, runs from "the plains of northern Syria" in the north, through the Red Sea, to Mozambique in the south. The term remains in use in the fields of geography, zoology, ecology, paleontology and other disciplines, but it is now rarely used in geology where the term "Afro-Arabian Rift System" is preferred, which describes the series of geological structures that have given rise to the geographical feature. Great Rift Valley is also often used to refer to valleys, such as the Kenyan Rift Valley, within the East African Rift system.
The term was introduced by British geologist John Walter Gregory in 1896, following on from the work of Austrian geologist Eduard Suess, who first proposed the existence of a linked set of features extending from Syria to Mozambique. 


Geology
The Afro-Arabian Rift (AAR) is a series of major geological structures that have created the observed topographic features that make up the Great Rift Valley. The northern part of the AAR is formed by the Dead Sea Transform (DST) (also known as the Dead Sea or Levantine rift), the transform type boundary between the Arabian plate and the African (Nubian) plate. It extends southwards from the Marash triple junction in southeastern Turkey, where it meets the East Anatolian Fault, to the mouth of the Gulf of Aqaba where it joins with the Red Sea Rift. The dominant displacement along the DST is left-lateral strike-slip, with transtension along the southern part, transpression in the central section in Lebanon and local transtension within overall transpression in the northern part. Transtension has produced a series of pull-apart basins, the Dead Sea, Sea of Galilee, Hula basin and the Ghab basin. The transpression has led to the uplift of the Anti-Lebanon Mountains and Mount Lebanon either side of the Beqaa Valley.
The Red Sea Rift is a mid-ocean ridge that accommodates the increasing separation between the Nubian and Arabian plates. The southeastern end of the Red Sea Rift links to both the western end of the Aden Ridge and the northern end of the East African Rift system (EARS), at the Afar triple junction.
Sited next to the triple junction, the Afar triangle is an area of thinned and heavily intruded continental crust. The EARS continues to the south of the Afar triangle as the Main Ethiopian Rift passing through the strongly uplifted Ethiopian Highlands. Further south, the EARS splits into two main parts, the western Albertine Rift and the eastern Gregory Rift that pass to either side of the Victoria microplate, before joining again to the north of Lake Malawi. The EARS continues southwards to the coast along Lake Malawi and the Urema Graben. The Main Ethiopian and Gregory rifts are associated with major off-axis volcanism and many of the active basins within the rift are at least part filled with volcanic products. The Albertine Rift and its southward continuation into Mozambique are dominated by the formation of half-graben basins with major subsidence and flank uplifts.


Geography


Asian section
The most northerly part of the GRV is the Ghab Plain, developed above the Ghab basin, along the valley of the Orontes River in northern Syria. The next section to the south of the Ghab plain is the Beqaa valley, which contains two rivers, the Orontes river, which drains northwards and the Litani, which drains southwestwards. At the southern end of the valley, where the Litani river turns abruptly westwards, it comes within 5 km of the Hisbai river, part of the headwaters of the Jordan river. Beyond the Beqaa valley, the remaining part of the GRF in Asia is known as the Jordan Rift Valley, extending down to the Red Sea. The Hula valley, which lies above the Hula basin, is a nearly completely flat valley at about 70 m elevation, confined between the drainage basin of the many tributaries of the Jordan
grok_lead: The Great Rift Valley is a series of contiguous geographic depressions stretching approximately 6,000 kilometers from the Levant in western Asia, through the Red Sea and East Africa, to the coastal lowlands of Mozambique. The East African portion, also known as the East African Rift, is an active continental rift system formed by the divergence of the Somali and Nubian plates along a tectonic boundary, representing one of the few places on Earth where the African continent is actively splitting apart, driven by upwelling mantle material that thins the lithosphere and triggers faulting and volcanism. The valley features dramatic fault-block escarpments rising thousands of meters, a chain of elongated rift lakes such as Tanganyika and Malawi, and scattered volcanic peaks, creating a diverse landscape that spans altitudes from below sea level in the Afar Depression to over 5,000 meters on the Ethiopian Plateau. Geologically, the rift system originated around 30 million years ago during the Oligocene epoch, with rifting initiating in the northern Afar region due to a mantle plume and propagating southward at rates of several centimeters per year. It comprises two primary branches in East Africa âthe Eastern Rift, which runs through Kenya and Tanzania, and the Western Rift, extending along the borders of Uganda, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Malawi âenclosing the elevated East African Plateau and linked by accommodation zones of transverse faults. Ongoing tectonic activity produces frequent earthquakes, geothermal hotspots like those in the Olkaria fields of Kenya, and voluminous volcanism, including the formation of the Ethiopian Highlands and isolated massifs such as Mount Kilimanjaro, which stands at 5,895 meters as an inactive stratovolcano. Over time, continued extension could lead to the creation of new ocean crust, similar to the processes observed in the Red Sea arm of the rift. The Great Rift Valley holds profound significance for understanding human evolution, serving as the " cradle of humankind " where key paleoanthropological discoveries have illuminated the origins of the genus Homo and earlier hominins. Iconic sites such as Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania and the Turkana Basin in Kenya have yielded fossils and early stone tools dating back 2.6 million years, revealing bipedalism, brain expansion, and behavioral adaptations in fluctuating savanna environments. These findings include Australopithecus afarensis (e.g., the 3.2-million-year-old " Lucy " skeleton from Hadar, Ethiopia). Preserved in volcanic ash layers that enable precise radiometric dating, they demonstrate how rift-related climate variabilityâsuch as wet-dry cycles influencing lake levels and vegetationâdrove speciation and dispersal events among early humans over the past 7 million years. Ecologically, the rift's topographic and climatic diversity fosters exceptional biodiversity, with its alkaline soda lakes, freshwater rift lakes, and montane forests supporting endemic species and high endemism rates. Lake Tanganyika, the world's longest freshwater lake at 673 kilometers, harbors over 250 species of cichlid fishes that have undergone rapid adaptive radiation, while the Ethiopian Highlands âbisected by the riftâhost unique flora and fauna, including gelada baboons and Ethiopian wolves, in a recognized biodiversity hotspot. Migratory herds of wildebeest and zebras traverse the Serengeti plains within the Eastern Rift, sustaining one of Africa's most iconic ecosystems, though human activities like agriculture and urbanization pose ongoing threats to this natural heritage.
